title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
directAnswer: Reverse the list in consecutive blocks of k, but only if a full block of k nodes remains — a leftover tail of fewer than k stays as-is. Before reversing each block, scan ahead k nodes to confirm there are enough; if not, stop. Reverse that block with the standard prev/curr flip, then stitch the previous block's tail to this block's new head and remember the current block's old head as the next block's tail anchor. Iterative gives O(n) time and O(1) space; the recursive version is the same logic with O(n/k) stack depth.

remember.pattern: Block-wise in-place reversal with a 'k nodes remain?' guard
remember.formula:
dummy -> head; groupPrev = dummy
loop:
    kth = walk k nodes from groupPrev; if kth is null: break  # leftover < k
    groupNext = kth.next
    reverse [groupPrev.next .. kth] with prev = groupNext
    tmp = groupPrev.next      # old head -> becomes block tail
    groupPrev.next = kth      # stitch prev block tail -> new head
    groupPrev = tmp
return dummy.next
rules: **Check first**: confirm k full nodes remain before reversing; a trailing block of fewer than k is left **unchanged**.
Use a **dummy node** so the first block's reversal (which changes the head) needs no special case.
Per block, reconnect two links: previous block's tail → this block's **new head** (the old kth node), and this block's **new tail** (old head) → the next block.
Initialise the flip's `prev` to **groupNext** so the reversed block's tail already points at the next block.
Recursive version: recurse on the remainder, then reverse the front k and link `head.next` to the recursive result; base case is **fewer than k nodes → return head**.
whenToUse: Reverse a linked list in fixed-size chunks
Any per-block in-place pointer rewrite with a remainder rule
Batch/window processing of a singly linked list
Follow-ups to Reverse Linked List and Reverse Linked List II
antiSignals: Reverse a single arbitrary segment → Reverse Linked List II (one window)
Reverse the whole list → Reverse Linked List (no blocks)
k = 2 only → Swap Nodes in Pairs (a special case)
remember.takeaway: Reverse Nodes in k-Group is partial reversal generalized to a stream of blocks. The hard part isn't the flip — it's the bookkeeping that stitches block N's tail to block N+1, plus the 'enough nodes left?' guard. Nail the iterative O(1)-space version and the recursive form falls out for free.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can reverse a linked list in fixed-size groups in place, check that a full group remains before reversing, and correctly re-link consecutive groups without losing nodes or creating cycles.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reversing a trailing partial group that should be left alone, mis-stitching the boundary between groups, or forgetting that the old group head becomes the group's tail (the anchor for the next group).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with the iterative O(1)-space solution, isolate the 'k nodes remain?' check, articulate the two boundary relinks per group, and offer the clean recursive version while naming its O(n/k) stack cost.

problemStatement:
Given the `head` of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list `k` at a time, and return *the modified list*.

`k` is a positive integer and is less than or equal to the length of the linked list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of `k` then **left-out nodes, in the end, should remain as they are**.

You may not alter the values in the list's nodes, only nodes themselves may be changed.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is n
Follow-up: Can you solve the problem in O(1) extra memory space?
understanding: We reverse the list in consecutive blocks of exactly k nodes. The final block is reversed only if it has all k nodes; otherwise it's left untouched. We rewire pointers in place and never copy values — only node links change.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens to a trailing group with fewer than k nodes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's left as-is, in its original order. Only complete groups of k are reversed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I do it in O(1) extra space?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the iterative version uses a constant number of pointers. The recursive version is cleaner but costs O(n/k) stack frames.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to swap node values instead of relinking?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the prompt forbids altering values; only the node links may change. So this must be a pointer-rewiring solution.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is k guaranteed to be at least 1 and at most n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. k = 1 is a no-op (each group of one reverses to itself), and k = n reverses the entire list once.

examples.explanation: Reverse [1,2]→[2,1] and [3,4]→[4,3]; the trailing [5] has fewer than k=2 nodes, so it stays.
Reverse the first 3 → [3,2,1]; the remaining [4,5] is shorter than k=3 and is left unchanged.
A single full group of 4 reverses entirely.

approaches.name: Iterative — Check, Flip, Stitch (O(1) Space)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the answer to the O(1)-memory follow-up. Phrase it as 'for each block, verify k nodes remain, reverse it, then wire the previous block's tail to this block's new head'.
hints: Use a dummy node before head. Keep a groupPrev pointer at the node just before the block you're about to reverse.
Before reversing, walk k steps from groupPrev to find the k-th node of the block. If you fall off the end (null), fewer than k nodes remain — stop and leave them as is.
Reverse the block, then reconnect: groupPrev.next should point to the block's new head (the old k-th node), and the block's old head (now its tail) becomes the next groupPrev.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited a constant number of times — once by the 'k nodes remain?' scan and once by the reversal — so O(n) total. Only a fixed set of pointers is used, giving O(1) extra space (the answer to the follow-up).
approaches.explanation:
This is partial reversal applied repeatedly, with careful hand-offs between blocks.

**The dummy node and groupPrev.** A `dummy` in front of `head` means the very first block's reversal (which changes the list head) needs no special case — `groupPrev` simply starts at the dummy. Throughout, `groupPrev` is the invariant 'node immediately before the block I'm reversing'. After each block it advances to the block's new tail, ready for the next block.

**Check before you flip — the remainder rule.** The defining twist of this problem is that a trailing block of fewer than `k` nodes must be left alone. So before touching any pointers, we walk `k` steps from `groupPrev` to locate the block's `k`-th node (`kth`). If that walk runs off the end into `null`, there aren't `k` nodes left, and we `break` — leaving the remainder untouched. Doing the check *first* is what prevents accidentally reversing a partial tail.

**Reverse the block with prev seeded to groupNext.** Once we know a full block exists, `groupNext = kth.next` is the start of whatever follows. We then run the standard three-pointer flip over the block — but we initialise `prev = groupNext` instead of `null`. That single choice makes the block's *tail* (its old first node) point directly at the next block as a side effect of the reversal, so one of the two boundary links is handled automatically. The flip stops when `curr` reaches `groupNext`.

**Stitch the two boundaries.** After the flip, the block is internally reversed and its tail already points to `groupNext`. Two assignments finish the wiring: we capture the block's old head (`tmp = groupPrev.next`) which is now the block's tail, set `groupPrev.next = kth` to connect the previous block to this block's new head, and finally move `groupPrev = tmp` so it sits on the new tail for the next iteration. Capturing `tmp` *before* overwriting `groupPrev.next` is essential — otherwise you lose the handle on the new tail.

**Why this answers the follow-up.** There's no recursion and no auxiliary structure — just a handful of pointers reused across blocks. That's genuine O(1) extra space, which is exactly what the 'O(1) memory' follow-up is probing.
approaches.insight: The reversal itself is the easy part; the problem is really about *bookkeeping between blocks*. Two facts carry the whole solution: the block's old head becomes its tail (so it's the anchor that links to the next block), and seeding `prev = groupNext` pre-wires the tail to the suffix. Hold those two and the stitching is mechanical.

code.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def reverseKGroup(self, head: ListNode, k: int) -> ListNode:
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    group_prev = dummy
    while True:
        # 1) Verify k nodes remain; kth is the block's last node.
        kth = group_prev
        for _ in range(k):
            kth = kth.next
            if kth is None:
                break
        if kth is None:
            break  # fewer than k left -> leave as is
        group_next = kth.next
        # 2) Reverse the block; prev seeded to group_next wires the tail.
        prev, curr = group_next, group_prev.next
        while curr != group_next:
            nxt = curr.next
            curr.next = prev
            prev = curr
            curr = nxt
        # 3) Stitch: prev block tail -> new head; advance group_prev.
        tmp = group_prev.next   # old head, now the block's tail
        group_prev.next = kth   # kth is the block's new head
        group_prev = tmp
    return dummy.next

approaches.name: Recursive — Reverse the Front, Recurse the Rest
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the clean alternative once the iterative version is out. Note the O(n/k) stack cost so it's an informed trade-off, not an oversight.
hints: First check whether k nodes exist starting at head. If not, return head unchanged — that's both the base case and the remainder rule.
If they do, reverse just the first k nodes with the standard flip. After the flip, head is the tail of this block and the (k+1)-th node starts the rest.
Recurse on the (k+1)-th node and attach its result to head.next, then return the new head of this block.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is reversed exactly once across all recursive calls → O(n) time. There's one stack frame per block, and there are n/k blocks, so the recursion depth (and stack space) is O(n/k).
approaches.explanation:
The recursive form expresses the same algorithm as 'reverse one block, then trust recursion for the rest'.

**The base case doubles as the remainder rule.** We first walk `k` nodes from `head`. If we hit `null` before counting `k`, this block is incomplete, so we return `head` unmodified. That single check serves two purposes: it's the recursion's termination condition *and* it enforces 'leftover fewer than k stays as-is'. No separate end-of-list handling is needed.

**Reverse the front k, leaving head as the tail.** When a full block exists, we run the classic `prev`/`curr` flip exactly `k` times over the first block. After the loop, `prev` is the block's new head (the old `k`-th node), `head` is the block's tail (it hasn't moved, but everything now points the other way), and `curr` sits on the `(k+1)`-th node — the head of the remainder.

**The recursive leap of faith.** We assume `reverseKGroup(curr, k)` correctly k-group-reverses everything *after* this block and returns the head of that processed remainder. Our job is only to attach it: `head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, k)`. Because `head` is this block's tail, pointing its `next` at the recursively-processed remainder seamlessly joins block to block. Then we return `prev`, this block's new head, which the *previous* frame attaches in turn.

**Why it costs O(n/k) stack.** There's one frame per block, and the recursion only goes one level deeper per block (not per node), so the depth is the number of blocks, `n/k`. For `n ≤ 5000` that's fine, but it's strictly more memory than the iterative O(1) version — which is precisely why the iterative form is the answer to the O(1)-space follow-up, and this is the elegant 'if recursion is allowed' alternative.
approaches.insight: Recursion makes the block hand-off implicit: 'head is the tail, so head.next = (the rest, already solved)'. The trade is conceptual clarity for O(n/k) stack frames. Naming that trade out loud — 'cleaner, but not O(1) space' — shows you understand the cost, which is exactly what a hard-tagged problem wants.

code.python:
def reverseKGroup(self, head: ListNode, k: int) -> ListNode:
    # Base case + remainder rule: fewer than k nodes -> leave as is.
    node = head
    for _ in range(k):
        if node is None:
            return head
        node = node.next
    # Reverse the first k nodes.
    prev = None
    curr = head
    for _ in range(k):
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    # head is now this block's tail; link it to the processed remainder.
    head.next = self.reverseKGroup(curr, k)
    return prev  # new head of this block

pitfalls: Reversing before checking for k nodes — would reverse a partial trailing block.
Forgetting head.next = recursion — disconnects the blocks.
Returning head instead of prev — returns the tail of the block, not its new head.
Ignoring the O(n/k) stack cost when O(1) space is required.

commonMistakes: Reversing a trailing group with fewer than k nodes instead of leaving it unchanged.
Mis-stitching consecutive groups — losing the suffix or creating a cycle.
Forgetting that the old group head becomes the group's tail (the next group's anchor).
Using recursion when O(1) extra space is explicitly required.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reversing an incomplete trailing group
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The spec says a leftover group of fewer than k nodes stays as-is. If you reverse without first confirming k nodes remain, the tail comes out reversed and wrong.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Losing the new tail when stitching
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The old group head becomes the group's tail and is the anchor the next group attaches to. If you overwrite groupPrev.next before saving it, you lose that handle and can't advance correctly.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
groupPrev.next = kth;          // overwrote the old head reference
ListNode tmp = groupPrev.next;  // this is now kth, NOT the old head
groupPrev = tmp;                // wrong anchor for the next group
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
ListNode tmp = groupPrev.next;  // capture old head (new tail) FIRST
groupPrev.next = kth;           // then stitch to the new head
groupPrev = tmp;                // advance to the correct anchor

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursive version returns the tail, not the head
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After reversing the front k nodes, prev is the block's new head and head is its tail. Returning head returns the tail, so the caller links to the wrong node and the list breaks.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
prev = None; curr = head
for _ in range(k):
    nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nxt
head.next = self.reverseKGroup(curr, k)
return head    # head is the TAIL now — wrong
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
prev = None; curr = head
for _ in range(k):
    nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nxt
head.next = self.reverseKGroup(curr, k)
return prev    # prev is the new head

patternNote: Block-wise in-place reversal with a remainder guard. A dummy node erases the first-block edge case; each block reverses with the standard flip and is stitched to its neighbours via two boundary links. Iterative is O(1) space (the follow-up answer); recursion trades O(n/k) stack for clarity. Same family as Reverse Linked List, Reverse Linked List II, and Swap Nodes in Pairs.
